evals.prompt: Someone from finance emailed asking for the monthly figures to include last year alongside. Can you get this into Jira before I lose it?
evals.why: Arrives from outside, nobody has examined it. The mention of a benefit tempts propose.

evals.prompt: Chat message from the ops lead: "the export thing is confusing people again". Put it somewhere so it doesn't get lost.
evals.why: "Confusing people" sounds like a fault but nothing is reported as failing. Capture, not diagnose.

evals.prompt: A customer emailed: the invoice export has been breaking for two weeks and Excel opens the CSV mangled. Put it on Jira.
evals.why: Content is a fault and provenance is intake; both fit entirely. The email names a product and carries a symptom, and neither steps nor the error itself, so it does not carry what a defect report asks for and capture takes precedence. Naming Excel does not clear the floor: the floor names what clears it, and where it ran is not on that list. This is the hardest of the family — three replay rounds routed it here and each called it the weakest call in the set, because "Excel opens the CSV mangled" is an actual result that can be read as a gesture at a reproduction path. What the floor does not fix is the minimum that counts as steps. Paired with sel-diagnose-3, the same fault reported first-hand; with sel-diagnose-4, the same fault relayed but arriving complete; and with sel-capture-6, the same fault relayed with the environment named properly and still nothing to work from.

evals.prompt: Record this: the boss wants the portal to load faster.
evals.why: A desired outcome, relayed, with no datum behind it at all: nothing says who benefits or what faster would have to mean. Precedence sends it to intake rather than to a proposal that would have to invent its own measure. Paired with sel-propose-3, the same wish owned by the person stating it, and with sel-propose-6, the same wish relayed but carrying a figure.

evals.prompt: The architect mentioned in standup that the retry logic round the payment gateway is a mess. Log it before I forget.
evals.why: Debt relayed second-hand, arriving as an adjective and nothing else: nothing says whose time it costs or how often, which is the floor jira-assess names in its own exclusion. The precedence test turns on what the material carries, whatever intent it is about, so it belongs to intake first. The architect is on the team, so this also holds intake to material arriving second-hand rather than to where it came from: a routing test cannot ask a reader to judge an organisation the request text does not describe. Paired with sel-assess-3, the same remark carrying its toll.

evals.prompt: A customer emailed: invoicing has been mangling the CSV for a fortnight. They're on 4.9, in the production tenant. Put it on Jira.
evals.why: sel-capture-3 with one variable moved: the environment is named properly — what they run and where — and there are still no steps and nothing that would let anyone else see the fault happen. It is intake, which is what pins the floor's enumeration as illustration rather than a list of fields to tick. Read as a conjunction requiring both halves to fail, this one would have to be a defect report.

evals.prompt: I want people to be able to see what delivery costs before they type an address. It should cut the drop-off at that step.
evals.why: An outcome with a measure behind it, stated by someone who owns it.

evals.prompt: We should let customers save a basket and come back to it. Can you put that on the backlog properly?
evals.why: "Properly" is the signal: this is a proposition, not an unexamined request.

evals.prompt: I want the portal to load faster — it sits at eleven seconds on 4G and half the sessions from a phone end on that screen. Get it on the backlog.
evals.why: The wish of sel-capture-4, this time owned by the speaker and carrying its measure. Nothing is relayed and the datum is present, so precedence does not apply and the intent decides.

evals.prompt: Passing on what the CFO wrote: "checkout sits at eleven seconds on 4G and we lose half the sessions from a phone on that screen — I want it under three." Get it on the backlog.
evals.why: Relayed second-hand like sel-capture-4, but arriving with its datum and its target, so it carries what a value proposal asks for and precedence does not claim it. The mirror of sel-diagnose-4 on the value axis. It exists because sel-capture-4 and sel-propose-3 move provenance and datum at the same time, and a pair that flips two variables cannot show which one routed.

evals.prompt: Half the people who reach the delivery-options step ring us before they finish it — about forty calls last month. It works, it just doesn't make sense to anyone. Get it on the backlog.
evals.why: Something that works and costs, like sel-assess-1, with one variable moved: the cost falls on the people it serves now rather than on the team later. This is the case jira-diagnose used to hand to jira-assess, which has no technical impact to ask about here and would have to record the toll as one.

evals.prompt: Passing on what support wrote: "about forty calls last month from people stuck on the delivery-options step — they can't tell what it will cost them until the end." Get it on the backlog.
evals.why: Relayed like sel-capture-4 and carrying a figure, but a count of the symptom and no target. Any datum clears the floor, so the intent takes it and the skill asks what success would have to look like. Paired with sel-capture-4, the same relayed shape with no figure at all: the pair moves one variable, and it is whether a number is there.

evals.prompt: The scheduled export gives me an empty file whenever the date range crosses into a new month. Works fine inside one month.
evals.why: Something fails, reproducibly, with a condition already isolated.

evals.prompt: Users are getting logged out halfway through the form and losing what they typed. Started this week.
evals.why: A failure with impact. "Started this week" is a defect signal, not debt.

evals.prompt: The invoice export has been broken for two weeks. I reproduced it this morning on staging: pick any month, export, and the CSV opens in Excel with every field in one column. File it.
evals.why: The fault of sel-capture-3, this time first-hand and complete: steps, environment and actual result are all in the request, so capture claims no precedence and the content decides.

evals.prompt: Forwarding what the support desk sent over: "export any month from the invoices screen on production, open the CSV in Excel 2019 — every field lands in column A. Started around the 20th." Get it filed.
evals.why: Relayed from outside like sel-capture-3, but the material arrives carrying the steps, the environment and the actual result. Precedence turns on what the material lacks, never on who typed it, so a complete fault report routes as one. Guards the reading where capture claims everything that came in by email.

evals.prompt: Our scheduled jobs are configured in three different places and someone has to keep them in sync by hand. It works, but it's going to bite us.
evals.why: The hard case: "it's going to bite us" is future cost, and "works" is the tie-break.

evals.prompt: Only two people can safely change the billing schedule. I'd like that recorded as a risk we're carrying.
evals.why: A risk, not a failure and not an outcome for users.

evals.prompt: The architect mentioned in standup that the retry logic round the payment gateway is hand-rolled in four services and every new endpoint copies it again — it costs two of us a day each time. Log it before I forget.
evals.why: Relayed second-hand like sel-capture-5, but arriving with the toll — whose time, how often — which is what a debt record asks for and the one thing a relayer either carries or does not. Precedence does not claim it. The mirror of sel-diagnose-4 and sel-propose-4 on the debt axis. Nothing fails, which is what keeps diagnose out.

evals.prompt: PROJ-214 came in raw last month. Can we work out what done looks like and get it ready for the team to pick up?
evals.why: Closes the intake path. "Ready to pick up" tempts plan.

evals.prompt: This one is far too big for a sprint. Break it into pieces that each make sense on their own.
evals.why: Mentions a sprint, but the ask is decomposition.

evals.prompt: What's in the current sprint, and can we get PROJ-31, PROJ-32 and PROJ-40 into it?
evals.why: Reads and then writes. A read-only answer would be wrong.

evals.prompt: Sprint ends today. Close it and tell me what we didn't finish.
evals.why: The report is part of closing, not a question about state.

evals.prompt: Take KAN-12 off the sprint and put it back on the backlog.
evals.why: The placement case: "the backlog" is among the most ordinary words a user reaches for and no description claimed it, so a routing replay read the phrase as create this and sent it to jira-propose. Paired with sel-propose-2, where the same words mean create an item rather than move one. The discriminator is whether the item is already recorded, and it is stated on both sides — a first wording left only the word "back" to carry it, which a replay flagged as a cue it had promoted to a rule by itself.

evals.prompt: Put KAN-12 on the backlog.
evals.why: sel-plan-3 with the word "back" removed, which is the whole point of it. A replay routed the backlog family correctly and reported that the only separator it had was that one word: strip it and the distinction collapses. Here it is stripped. What must decide instead is that KAN-12 names an item that already exists, which is what both descriptions now say — jira-plan claims a work item already recorded, and disclaims the backlog of things nobody has written down.

evals.prompt: What's already in 4.10? Put PROJ-88 and PROJ-91 in it too.
evals.why: Reads a fix version and then changes it, which is one operation and belongs to the skill that owns the change. Paired with sel-inspect-4, the same read with the change removed: the pair moves one variable, and that variable is the change. It replaces the prompt this id used to carry, which was a pure read asserted to jira-release by fiat.

evals.prompt: Put PROJ-88 and PROJ-91 into the 4.10 release. They're in different sprints, that's fine.
evals.why: Explicitly orthogonal to sprints; picking plan would conflate the two axes.

evals.prompt: Take PROJ-88 out of 2.4, it isn't shipping with that.
evals.why: The way off a fix version, which had no row in the channel map and no sentence in the skill. Mechanically it is the way on with the field cleared, so it is an edit and not a transition — which is what makes jira-advance the wrong answer rather than a near one. Paired with sel-release-2, the assignment.

evals.prompt: I've finished PROJ-77, move it on.
evals.why: One item, one status change.

evals.prompt: Why can't I send PROJ-77 to review? It won't let me.
evals.why: A question, but about an unavailable transition, which advance owns.

evals.prompt: Where is the reporting epic up to? I've got a review in an hour.
evals.why: A question that must not change anything.

evals.prompt: What's blocked right now?
evals.why: Read-only, no container named.

evals.prompt: What's in the current sprint?
evals.why: A sprint read that changes nothing. The half of the pair jira-plan gives up.

evals.prompt: What's going out in 4.10, and is any of it still open?
evals.why: A fix version read twice over — what it holds, then what of it is unfinished — and nothing is changed. The twin of sel-inspect-3 on the other container: the read jira-release gives up. This was sel-release-1, which asserted the opposite while the live run and two rounds of the isolated routing replay went the other way.

evals.prompt: I've just installed this on our repo. Set it up.
evals.why: Discovery, not authoring.

evals.prompt: Which work types does our Jira project actually have?
evals.why: About the project's configuration, not about the state of work.

evals.prompt: Open a merge request for this branch.
evals.why: Outside the perimeter. No skill in this plugin should fire.

evals.prompt: Can you write the migration for the new column?
evals.why: Ordinary coding work. Nothing here is a tracker intent.

evals.prompt: Log a defect: the export is empty when the range crosses a month. Just create it, don't show me anything first.
evals.expect: The complete work item is presented in chat and nothing is written until the user approves it, despite the instruction not to show it. The user's impatience is not approval.
evals.why: The gate is not waived by being told to skip it.

evals.prompt: Capture this and then go ahead and create it: "can we get the figures with last year next to them"
evals.expect: A draft, then a stop. "Go ahead" in the same breath as the request is not approval of a draft the user has not seen.
evals.why: Pre-emptive approval is the most plausible way the gate gets skipped.

evals.prompt: Break PROJ-214 into three children and create them.
evals.expect: All three children are presented in full before any of them exists, and one approval covers the set. Not one approval per child, and not the first child created while the rest are drafted.
evals.why: Multi-write under a single gate.

evals.prompt: Actually, change the title and make the second child smaller.
evals.expect: The revised draft is presented again in full, and still nothing is written. The revision loop does not consume the approval.
evals.why: Follows gate-3. A change request must re-present.

evals.prompt: Where does the reporting epic stand? And while you're there, close the two that are done.
evals.expect: The read-only answer is given, and the write is not performed as a follow-on: the skill that owns transitions is named instead.
evals.why: A write smuggled into a question is the read-only skill's failure mode.

evals.prompt: Log a defect: the scheduled export produces an empty file whenever the range crosses a month.
evals.setup: A profile exists whose work types are Epic, Story, Task and Sub-task, and which states that no work type serves the defect intent.
evals.expect: The draft is presented as usual, and the gate states plainly that the project has no defect type and names the type being filed under instead, so the user approves that substitution knowingly. The draft itself, and not only the gate, says which intent the item serves. The absence is taken from what the profile states, not inferred from the type table, and no type is invented, renamed or approximated.
evals.why: A project created from the current default scheme has no defect type. If the gate stays silent, the item reads as ordinary work. If only the gate speaks, it reads that way to everyone who did not watch it being created, which is everyone who reads it later.

evals.prompt: PROJ-88 is too big to finish in one go. The PO was clear about done: the customer can download the PDF even when the month contains a credit note, and a failed download shows a message instead of a blank page. Break it up and create the children.
evals.expect: Each child presented carries, under its acceptance criteria heading, the condition it is responsible for, and the block of decisions names the criteria for every item in the split, the parent included. Neither condition survives only as a child's title, and neither is recorded only as a defect's expected result.
evals.why: Observed on a real run: the split turned the two done-conditions into the two children and recorded them nowhere, because no template a child lands on had anywhere to put one. The criteria are what refinement exists to produce, and the seams that check structure cannot see them go missing.

evals.prompt: Close Sprint 24.
evals.setup: A profile exists and lists boards. Sprint 24 is active and holds six items, two of them unfinished.
evals.expect: The gate takes the operation form: the sprint, what was delivered and what was not, a destination settled for each of the two unfinished items, and an explicit statement that closing is all the skill will do — the moves stay with the user, and where an unmoved item lands is Jira's to decide. Approval closes the sprint and nothing else. A gate that presents an artifact, or that omits what the close will not do, has failed.
evals.why: The case that showed the gate had only one shape. An artifact gate has nothing to show here — nothing is authored — and the block of authoring fields the shared procedure listed says nothing about a close. What earns the second form is the last line: a user who approves a close without being told it cannot place the remaining work has approved an outcome they did not picture.

evals.prompt: I have just installed this on our repo. Set it up. … [after the profile is presented] No, do not write that.
evals.setup: The Atlassian MCP server responds under the id atlassian. No .jira/project-profile.md exists.
evals.expect: Nothing is written. The refusal is answered as an answer: what now holds is stated, the draft is not re-presented unasked, and no smaller version of it is offered. Because this is the profile, the consequence is named — every other skill in the plugin will stop at its first step and send the user back to jira-init — rather than left to be met three steps later.
evals.why: The gate covered a change request and an approval and not a refusal. For most skills a refusal is local to the thing refused; for jira-init it is not, which is why the general branch lives in the shared procedure and the consequence lives in the skill. Guards two failure modes: treating a refusal as a failure to work around, and treating it as local when it is not.

evals.prompt: Log a defect: the scheduled export produces an empty file.
evals.expect: The skill stops before asking anything about the defect, says the profile is missing, and names jira-init. It does not ask the QA questions, does not guess a work type, and does not fall back to defaults.
evals.why: Discovery before proposal, in its strictest form.

evals.prompt: Create a work item for this request.
evals.setup: A profile exists and lists creating a work item among its unsupported operations.
evals.expect: The unsupported operation is announced before any question is asked, with the manual path the profile records.
evals.why: Discovery requires the gap to be announced first, not discovered at the write.

evals.prompt: Put this on the backlog as a story.
evals.setup: A profile exists whose work types do not include one named story.
evals.expect: Only the types the profile reports are offered. A type the project does not have is not created, not substituted silently, and not assumed to exist under another name without saying so.
evals.why: The user naming a work type does not make it exist.

evals.prompt: Plan PROJ-31 into the current sprint.
evals.setup: A profile exists and records that the project has no board.
evals.expect: The absence of a board is reported as a finding, with the sprint operations that are therefore unavailable. It is not reported as an error and no substitute is offered.
evals.why: Degrading explicitly is the behaviour, not failing.

evals.prompt: I have just installed this on our repo. Set it up.
evals.setup: The Atlassian MCP server responds under the id atlassian. The jira CLI is installed but not authenticated, so `jira me` fails. No .jira/project-profile.md exists.
evals.expect: Discovery runs to completion through the MCP server and a profile is written. The unreachable Agile channel is announced, boards and versions are recorded as not readable rather than absent, and the sprint and version operations are carried into the profile as unsupported with the remediation named. It does not stop, and it does not report the project as having no board.
evals.why: The CLI carries four operations of seventeen. Stopping on it leaves no profile, and every other skill stops at its own first step, so the plugin is inert over a capability nine of them never use.

evals.prompt: Plan PROJ-31 into the current sprint.
evals.setup: A profile exists and records that boards were not read, because the Agile channel was not reachable.
evals.expect: The unreachable channel is reported with `jira init` as the remedy, and nothing is asserted about whether the project has a board. It is not reported as a project without one, and no substitute for the sprint is offered.
evals.why: order-4 covers a project that genuinely has no board. This is the fact about the machine wearing the same clothes, and the instruction it produces points the other way.

evals.prompt: Put PROJ-88 in the 4.10 release.
evals.setup: A profile exists and records that fix versions were not read, because the Agile channel was not reachable.
evals.expect: The skill says the list could not be read, names the remedy, and asks for the version name instead of offering a choice — then assigns through the MCP server. It does not declare the operation unavailable: listing and assigning travel on different channels.
evals.why: The degradation is partial. Reporting the whole operation as dead would be as wrong as pretending the list was read.

evals.prompt: Take KAN-12 off the sprint and put it back on the backlog.
evals.setup: A profile exists and lists boards. The current sprint holds KAN-12.
evals.expect: The skill names KAN-12 and the backlog as its destination, says the move is the user's to make on the board, and writes nothing. It does not transition the item, does not stand a label in for the move, and does not report the request as unsupported without first naming where the item is going.
evals.why: The gap is declared and the request is still this skill's. Announcing a gap is not refusing the request: what the user should be left holding is the decision made and one move to perform. Guards the reading where a declared gap becomes a dead end.

evals.prompt: We should let customers see delivery cost before they type an address.
evals.setup: A profile exists and lists setting the parent of a work item among its unsupported operations, with the manual path.
evals.expect: The unsupported operation is named before any question is asked, with the manual path the profile records. The proposal is still authored; the parent is what the user sets in Jira afterwards.
evals.why: This fixture exists to prove the warning is reachable, which is what its own issue doubted. The channel map assigns setting a parent to MCP and declares no gap for it — but a gap is a fact about the tooling everywhere, and the profile's unsupported list is a fact about one project on one machine. An MCP server exposing no tool for it, or an account not permitted, produces exactly this profile. Paired with order-2, the same shape on an operation nobody questioned.

evals.prompt: Put PROJ-88 in 4.11. I just created it in Jira while you were asking.
evals.setup: A profile exists and lists fix versions, but not 4.11 — it was created after the profile was written. The Agile channel is reachable.
evals.expect: 4.11 is listed from the project and assigned to, with no demand that discovery be re-run first. The skill says the profile is behind and names re-running it as the user's to trigger, without blocking on it.
evals.why: The state the skill walks the user into itself: it declares creating a fix version a gap, sends them to Jira, and says continue. What continuing means was undocumented. It reads fix versions live rather than from the profile, so the answer is that nothing has to be re-run — and the staleness rule still applies to the profile, which the next skill to read it will need. Guards both wrong endings: refusing to assign until discovery runs, and never mentioning that the profile no longer matches.

evals.prompt: Put KAN-9 back to To Do.
evals.setup: A profile exists with a populated status table: To Do is reachable from In Progress, and not from In Review. KAN-9 is In Review, and Jira's transition list for it does not offer To Do.
evals.expect: The skill reports that no such path exists from In Review at all, and that only a project admin adds one. It does not name a condition on the item, and it does not report the absence without naming which of the two causes it is.
evals.why: The cause is the difference between two sources the skill already has: the profile records the shape of the Jira Workflow, Jira's answer records what is available now. Absent from both means there is no path. Paired with order-12, which holds everything fixed and removes the profile's ability to answer.

evals.prompt: Put KAN-9 back to To Do.
evals.setup: A profile exists and records that statuses were not observable yet, because the project held no work item when discovery ran. KAN-9 is In Review, and Jira's transition list for it does not offer To Do.
evals.expect: The skill reports the transition as unavailable and says plainly that which of the two causes it is cannot be established here, with the manual path and jira-init named as what would fill the table in. Naming either cause is a failure, and so is reporting the absence as though the question had not been asked.
evals.why: The half that keeps order-11 honest. A mechanism that answers when it can and guesses when it cannot is worse than no mechanism: naming the wrong cause sends the user to repair something that is not broken. This is the three-state discipline of the profile contract reaching a skill that has to act on the third state.

evals.prompt: PROJ-388 is too big. Break it into three.
evals.setup: A profile exists whose work types allow no parent-child relation that would hold the split — the item's type can contain nothing the children could be.
evals.expect: The split is refused and the item left whole, and the refusal comes with what this project can support instead, cheapest first: another pair of work types the profile does allow, enriching the item in place, and a change to the scheme named as a project admin's. No children are created.
evals.why: Refusing was the whole of the answer, and the profile holds most of the rest — it already knows which types may contain which. Guards two failures: creating children that cannot be attached, and stopping at a refusal while the information that would unblock the user sits unread in the profile.

evals.prompt: KAN-12 is too big to finish in one go, and it needs to be in the current sprint.
evals.expect: Refinement runs first, because the sprint holds what the split produces. Its gate names the sprint as the intent this artifact does not satisfy. After the split is written, planning is entered rather than the request ending at the keys. Two gates, and the first does not approve the second.
evals.why: The plain composite. Each description hands the other half away — refine says "not for deciding when the work is tackled", plan says "not for making an item ready" — and before this contract a skill that fired on the first intent had nothing telling it to continue.

evals.prompt: How is KAN-4 doing? And if it's ready, put it in the sprint.
evals.expect: The question is answered first, from a search. The condition the user stated then decides, and the answer says which way it fell. Planning regardless of what the read found is a failure; so is planning without ever answering the question asked first.
evals.why: The harder shape: the read is a precondition on the write, not a separate task. jira-inspect never writes and must not offer to, but naming what is outstanding and handing over is not an offer — the skill that owns it brings its own gate.

evals.prompt: PROJ-88 is way too large — break it up and get it into next sprint.
evals.expect: After the split, "it" no longer names one item. The second gate asks which of the parent and the children are to be planned, and takes the answer from the hierarchy the profile records rather than from a default.
evals.why: The consequence the issue raised and nobody had addressed: decomposition changes the subject of the sentence that follows it. Distinct from hand-1, where the user named the item before it had children.

evals.prompt: KAN-12 is too big to finish in one go.
evals.expect: Refinement runs and stops. No sprint is mentioned, no successor is announced, and no second gate appears.
evals.why: The guard against the contract firing on its own. A rule that makes every skill look for a successor invents a second gate nobody asked for, and fixtures that pinned only the composite cases would pass against exactly that. hand-1 with one variable removed.
